extracted.intended_audience: students, theorists, and practitioners of political philosophy and public institutions (policymakers, reformers)
extracted.subtask_description: A compact set of evaluative criteria for judging and designing forms of government: what institutions must do and what qualities they must foster in a people to be 'good'. Emphasizes both the government's effect on citizens and the quality of its institutional machinery, adapted to a society's stage of development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to make its ordinances obeyed
rubrics_metrics.description: "Those who are unable to make their ordinances obeyed, can not be said to govern."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An indispensable attribute: the power to secure obedience is necessary (though not the ultimate purpose) because without it government cannot accomplish other ends. Example: for very uncivilized peoples a nearly despotic constitution may be required to teach obedience; the government must possess force but need not habitually use it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order (preservation of peace; cessation of private violence)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Order means the preservation of peace by the cessation of private violence."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order is a necessary condition/prerequisite of government but is not by itself the full criterion of excellence; the mere habit of submitting to authority can exist under very different qualities of administration. Order is best treated as part of the means to broader ends (it preserves existing goods and thereby supports Progress).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduciveness to Progress (increase of good and prevention of deterioration)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The best government is that which is most conducive to Progress." (Progress includes increase of existing goods and preventing retrogression.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progress is the appropriate overall criterion because it subsumes Order and Permanence. Progress also includes preventing decline; the same institutions that secure permanence often promote progress, but pursuit of new gains must not be at the expense of more valuable existing goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion of citizens' moral, intellectual, and active qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments should be judged by "the degree in which they tend to foster ... the various desirable qualities, moral and intellectual, or rather ... moral, intellectual, and active."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of desirable qualities: industry, integrity, justice, prudence, mental activity, enterprise, courage, originality. The first element of good government is its effect in increasing these qualities in the population because these qualities are the moving force of all government action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of the governmental machinery (organizational fitness)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The quality of the machinery itself; that is, the degree in which it is adapted to take advantage of the amount of good qualities which may at any time exist, and make them instrumental to the right purposes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A government's merit partly depends on how well institutions harness existing virtue and intelligence. Even abundant private virtue is wasted without appropriate institutional arrangements to bring it to bear on public affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicature and procedural standards (selection, procedure, publicity, evidence, access, detection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrangements such as "rendering the choice of the judges such as to obtain the highest average of virtue and intelligence; the salutary forms of procedure; the publicity which allows observation and criticism; the liberty of discussion and censure through the press; the mode of taking evidence; the facilities ... for obtaining access to the tribunals; the arrangements for detecting crimes and apprehending offenders."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are concrete elements of institutional machinery that determine whether judicial institutions turn private merit into reliable public justice. They are not ends themselves but instruments for eliciting truth, accountability, and fair administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative-office design: alignment of interest and duty; clear responsibility and checks
rubrics_metrics.description: "The ideally perfect constitution of a public office is that in which the interest of the functionary is entirely coincident with his duty."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tests: proper qualifications, promotion rules, division/distribution of business, methodical order, intelligible records, clear assignment of responsibility, and well-devised checks against negligence, favoritism, or jobbery. A good apparatus improves the effectiveness of whatever moral power exists among agents and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity plus active public oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: "Publicity ... is no impediment to evil, nor stimulus to good, if the public will not look at what is done; but without publicity, how could they either check or encourage what they were not permitted to see?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicity (transparency) only produces benefit if the public actually inspects and exerts opinion/pressure. Liberty of discussion and press are part of this; publicity enables the public to check or encourage officials and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative institutions as means of organizing intelligence and honesty
rubrics_metrics.description: "A representative constitution is a means of bringing the general standard of intelligence and honesty ... more directly to bear upon the government."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation amplifies the influence of the wisest and most virtuous members relative to other forms of organization. The better institutions are at organizing existing public virtue, the better the government will be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of form to the society's stage of development
rubrics_metrics.description: "The one indispensable merit of a government ... is that its operation on the people is favorable, or not unfavorable, to the next step which it is necessary for them to take in order to raise themselves to a higher level."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions must be adapted to the people's current character and capacities. Examples: near-despotism to teach obedience to 'savages'; 'leading-strings' parental despotism/aristocracy for slave populations being trained to self-government; representative institutions for more advanced peoples. Wrong-fit institutions can arrest further progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize damage to existing goods while pursuing progress
rubrics_metrics.description: "In seeking the good which is needed, no damage, or as little as possible, be done to that already possessed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progress that comes at a greater-than-equivalent loss of existing goods is not genuine progress. Policy choices should weigh gains and losses across kinds of goods (e.g., wealth vs. virtue) and avoid lopsided improvements that destroy broader well‑being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced personnel composition (mixture of caution and boldness)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Persons of both types ought to be included in it, that the tendencies of each may be tempered, in so far as they are excessive, by a due proportion of the other."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberative bodies should include both cautious (order-preserving) and bold (progress-seeking) temperaments so institutional tendencies are balanced. This can be achieved naturally by mixing ages and social positions, provided artificial rules don't disturb the balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twofold test: effect on people (education) and effect on affairs (machinery)
rubrics_metrics.description: "It consists partly of the degree in which they promote the general mental advancement of the community ... and partly of the degree of perfection with which they organize the moral, intellectual, and active worth already existing ..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge governments both by what they make of citizens (do they improve virtue, intelligence, activity?) and by what they do with citizens (is public business well-conducted?). These are distinct but interrelated functions; good machinery aids improvement, and improved citizens make institutions work better.
